title: Electronvolts: The Currency of Atomic Physics
h1: The electronvolt — energy at the atomic scale
description: Chemistry uses eV. Nuclear physics uses MeV. Particle physics uses GeV and TeV. Here is what an electronvolt actually is and where each scale fits.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

hero: One electronvolt is the energy an electron gains falling through 1 volt. That gives every particle physics energy a direct link to the voltage on the accelerator.
body: The electronvolt is not a joule and its size is not memorable — 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. But once you accept it as the natural unit for one electron falling through one volt, every atomic and nuclear energy fits into a simple ladder: chemistry at eV, X-rays at keV, nuclear reactions at MeV, and colliders at TeV.

> 1 eV = 1.602176634 × 10⁻¹⁹ J (exact since 2019 redefinition)
> 1 keV = 10³ eV; 1 MeV = 10⁶ eV; 1 GeV = 10⁹ eV; 1 TeV = 10¹²eV
> 1 eV/particle = 96.485 kJ/mol (chemistry conversion)

Hydrogen ionisation: 13.6 eV. Visible photon: 1.6–3.1 eV. Chemical bonds: 1–10 eV. X-ray photon: 1–100 keV. Nuclear binding per nucleon: ~8 MeV. Muon rest mass: 106 MeV. Proton rest mass: 938 MeV. Higgs boson: 125 GeV. LHC per-proton beam energy: 6.5 TeV.
## Mass and energy in the same unit

Particle physicists write masses in eV/c² because E = mc². The electron rest mass is 511 keV/c², the proton 938 MeV/c². The 'c²' is often dropped in speech ("a 125-GeV Higgs") because everyone knows what is meant. This convention lets you read a particle-physics paper without switching between joules, kilograms and eV.
## Worked example — an X-ray from a copper anode

The Kα emission of copper is 8.04 keV = 1.289 × 10⁻¹⁵ J per photon = 1.541 Å wavelength. A dental X-ray tube running at 70 kV produces bremsstrahlung with maximum photon energy 70 keV. Both are directly connected to the tube voltage — which is exactly why the unit was invented.
1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Atoms live at eV. Nuclei live at MeV. LHC lives at TeV. And mass in eV/c² is just energy divided by c².

faqs.a: kT = 1 eV when T = 11,605 K. Room temperature (300 K) corresponds to about 25.7 meV per particle — a useful anchor in semiconductor physics.

faqs.q: How does LHC compare to a lightning bolt?
faqs.a: A lightning bolt has ~10⁹ J of energy. LHC beam: 6.5 TeV per proton × 3 × 10¹⁴ protons = 3.1 × 10⁸ J — roughly a third of a lightning bolt, but focused on a beam 20 µm across.
No, but 'accepted for use with the SI'. Its value in joules is exact since 2019.
